name: Ambrosius-egen

location.address: Nørreskovvej, about 1 km southwest of Valdemars Slot, Tåsinge, near Svendborg, Denmark

access: Free, standing beside Nørreskovvej near Valdemars Slot on Tåsinge; no ticket or booking needed, ordinary public road/forest edge.
transport: No station on Tåsinge; reached by car or bicycle from Svendborg, across the Svendborgsund bridge, then along Nørreskovvej.
story:
A drill bit took three hundred years off this oak. In 1962 it was reckoned to be around 700 years old, the kind of figure that gets onto a sign and stays there. On 13 June 1997 someone bored a core into the trunk and counted the rings, and the answer came back at roughly 400, putting the tree's first year somewhere near 1600. Both figures are still on record. The ring count is the one to believe.

It carries the name of Ambrosius Stub, the poet, who worked as a scribe and tutor at Valdemars Slot a kilometre up the road around 1750 and is said to have done his reading and writing under it. By then the oak had already been standing for about a century and a half.

The trunk measures just under 7.5 metres round and the tree reaches about 20 metres. Denmark protected it as a natural monument in 1921. Surgeons cut rot out of it in 1973, and rot and fungus are still visible around the base, which is what a working four-hundred-year-old oak looks like when it is cared for rather than tidied away.

It stands at the forest edge on Nørreskovvej, on Tåsinge across the bridge from Svendborg. No gate, no ticket, no hunting for it: the road runs straight past.
container: new place: standalone (Tåsinge/Svendborg has no published city; nearest published Danish places are Copenhagen and Aarhus, both well over 100km away). Qualifies for the single-tree-place exception: nationally protected natural monument since 1921, named after a documented historical figure (poet Ambrosius Stub), independently dendro-dated, and already a listed destination on regional tourism sites. Suggest a new place 'Ambrosius-egen (Taasinge)' or fold into a future Svendborg/Taasinge page if other trees turn up nearby (Valdemars Slot park itself may hold more - worth a follow-up scout).

name: Svalebøgen

location.address: Stokkebro (main street), eastern end, Gjerrild, Norddjurs Kommune, Djursland, Denmark

access: Free, standing on the roadside at Stokkebro in Gjerrild village; benches sit beneath it and it is a known local picnic/geocache spot. No ticket or restriction, though the municipality has cordoned off parts of the immediate area at times for safety (see condition note).
transport: No train station; reached by car or bicycle, in the village of Gjerrild on Djursland.
story:
Local tradition says this beech started as a mouse's winter larder. A hoard of beech nuts buried in one spot germinated together, and the stems thickened into each other as they grew, which is why the thing standing at the eastern end of Stokkebro reads as one colossal tree and is really several. The Danish Dendrological Society put a tape around it in 1995 and got 12.52 metres, a figure that goes round the whole fused mass rather than any single stem.

Gjerrild calls it Denmark's oldest beech and its biggest tree. The age everyone repeats is about 300 years, and the village's own account says plainly that nobody knows exactly, so hold the number loosely.

It is coming apart, and there is no point pretending otherwise. One of the trunks collapsed on 9 June 2022. The municipality pruned the rest back for safety, warned that more looked likely to follow, and has cordoned off parts of the ground beneath it at times since. Gjerrild's own visitor page now describes the tree as in declining condition and still open to visitors, which is the honest version: an old beech letting go slowly, with benches under it and people still eating their lunch there.

The residents' association has planted a successor a little to the southeast. That one needs a couple of centuries. This is the one to go and stand under now.
container: new place: standalone (Gjerrild/Djursland has no published Danish city nearby; roughly 60km from Aarhus, beyond a reasonable day-trip radius, and nothing else published on Djursland). Qualifies for the single-tree-place exception on a real credential: locally and regionally documented as Denmark's oldest beech and largest tree, a named landmark with its own municipal safety announcements and a citizens' association succession-planting effort. Suggest a new place 'Svalebøgen (Gjerrild)'.
